title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for more than $1.4tn stock market debut
description: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.The artificial intelligence (A
body: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable. The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins. There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years. "Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary."Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind. It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so. Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money."AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".With additional reporting by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia

schema.headline: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for more than $1.4tn stock market debut

title: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia
description: The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the th
body: The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.He told the Telegraph, external he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade."Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal."I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry."As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.The BBC has approached the White House for comment.Having served in the military in Afghanistan, Harry said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters."Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties."War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

schema.headline: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia

title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
description: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kreml
body: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin. Whatever the outcome.Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed."We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."But what of those who are not at the table?Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe."We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

schema.headline: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin

title: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
description: Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, White
body: Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.There was no immediate comment from Google when approached by BBC News. On Sunday, his wife Laura had shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a handwritten message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account. The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material. The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, said she found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims."I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".In 2023, YouTube suspended Brand's channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy", shortly after he was accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013.The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site.Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

schema.headline: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say

title: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
description: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private resi
body: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

schema.headline: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour

title: Why children lie and it is important they do
description: Is your child lying to you? That might not be a bad thing Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Ada tries to sneakily eat co
body: Is your child lying to you? That might not be a bad thing Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Ada tries to sneakily eat cookie dough aged two when she thought her mum wasn't lookingByGeorge SandemanWhen drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development. "It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast. Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Juno also deceives her aged three by hiding under a table to eat marshmallowsYoung children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one. One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, external, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are ten months old. Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own."As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be. "Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.CBeebies Parenting DownloadClinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern explains why young children may lie and Traitors winner Rachel Duffy discusses how she encourages hers to tell the truth"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Ada, age two, deceives her mum by hiding in the bathroom to eat chocolate she had stolen"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains."This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent."All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth."[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast the she has been trying to do.Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka with her daughters Ada, now aged six, and Juno who is three years oldThe mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened."I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space."And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically."My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly. "I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."

schema.headline: Why children lie and it is important they do

title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
description: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president
body: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of AnthropicByTom Espiner and Lucy HookerBusiness reportersIn the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday. At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?Dario Amodei - $19.7bnImage source, Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIn 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profileDaniela Amodei - $19.8bnImage source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.Tom Brown - $20bnImage source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesTom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.Jack Clark $19.8bnImage source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty ImagesJack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.Jared Kaplan - $19.8bnImage source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesJared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.Chris Olah $19.9bn Image source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty ImagesChris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.Sam McCandlish - $19.9bnImage source, AnthropicSam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

schema.headline: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires

title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
description: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Gr
body: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype." But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building. "The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors. Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action. But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics."They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review."It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it."While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m). The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

schema.headline: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece

title: Fifa: Football Association explored Gianni Infantino legal challenge
description: The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.Bu
body: The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term.Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits."Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes."We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).However he has also said that the ability of European football associations to do so has been made harder by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin deciding to stand for a fourth term earlier this year. Ceferin reversed a previous insistence, in 2024, he would not seek re-election.The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.

schema.headline: Fifa: Football Association explored Gianni Infantino legal challenge

title: The tightest Premier League survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry for Man Utd, Sunderland and Crystal Palace
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?ByChris CollinsonBBC Sport statisticianDespite b
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?ByChris CollinsonBBC Sport statisticianDespite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.The bottom three may already be taking shapeLooking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.It's not all bad news for the bottom threeThis is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.Tight at the bottom - and in the middleWhile history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

schema.headline: The tightest Premier League survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry for Man Utd, Sunderland and Crystal Palace

title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa's maverick coach plans online watchalong
description: Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.I
body: Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.And he will not be short of virtual company.Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence."Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side."But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.It is not surprising.His feats with the team are astonishing.South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match. He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.Legally, he is across every possible loophole.There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off. Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town."He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social."I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards."He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions."Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement."Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.Some also see instinctive honesty rather than a premeditated ploy in his public speaking."He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials, external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.There is a wider question too.For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

schema.headline: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa's maverick coach plans online watchalong

title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
description: ByNoor Nanji & Zoe ConwayBBC NewsA former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has c
body: ByNoor Nanji & Zoe ConwayBBC NewsA former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claimsMcDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuseHope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him."I got the hell out of there," she says.Figure caption, Ex-McDonald's worker: "You need to fix it so it doesn't happen again"Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after."You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says."And why would you? That is literally a child still."Legal actionHundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees"."It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it  a lot safer, I think, as well.  And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out."And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"Image source, Getty ImagesThe claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard." A McDonald's spokesperson said they could not comment on the specifics of ongoing legal proceedings.In a statement, they said the company had "embedded an extensive set of robust and far-reaching initiatives" as part of its "steadfast commitment" to its staff, adding that this work continues."Any form of harassment, discrimination or inappropriate behaviour is unacceptable and has no place in our restaurants or offices. We are confident that with the guidance and partnership of external experts, we and our franchisees have industry leading safeguarding measures in place," the spokesperson added.

schema.headline: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'

title: Oyster photocard holders’ personal data accessed in TfL breach
description: The personal details of about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers have been accessed in a cyber breach, Transport for London (TfL) has said.Names, emai
body: The personal details of about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers have been accessed in a cyber breach, Transport for London (TfL) has said.Names, email and home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security questions and answers were compromised after "suspicious activity" was detected on the photocard website on Monday.TfL said it took the photocard system off line to limit access and had notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).It said no passwords, bank or payment card details or journey information were compromised.The photocard website remains offline, meaning customers cannot apply for or renew a photocard online until it is restored as an investigation continues.TfL said customers who needed to renew their photocard or discuss their journey history could contact customer services on 0343 222 1234. "Customers with Oyster photocards can continue to travel and we hope to restore services as quickly as possible."It is the second time in just over two years the system had been taken down because of a cyber incident.In September 2024, a cyber attack on TfL forced it to suspend new photocard applications for more than two months. TfL said at the time that about 5,000 customers had been contacted over possible access to their bank details, but the BBC later revealed that the data of about 10 million people had been stolen.The ICO cleared TfL of wrongdoing over its handling of that breach.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Oyster photocard holders’ personal data accessed in TfL breach

title: Birmingham City Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
description: Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure ac
body: Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags."The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said."It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like."Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

schema.headline: Birmingham City Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
